# Exact simultaneous Schur funding for three full tetrahedral rows

This note gives the remaining unique-noncentral incidence pattern and an exact scalar funding interface. It does not assert that the final scalar inequality always has the favorable sign.

Consider a positive-weight ordinary tetrahedral capacity maximum selected with the fewest active rows. Suppose precisely three rows X,Y,Z are active and full, their sum is 1 componentwise, and their common actual minimizing-section centroid b has exactly one coordinate b_h>1/3. All other coordinates are at most 1/3. All proper full-row minima are C2 and nondegenerate by the previously proved regularity theorem.

## 1. The admitted sign patterns

No minimizing cut can pass through vertex h: a section through that vertex is a triangle (possibly with an edge on a facet), and its centroid h-coordinate is at most 1/3. Every row therefore strictly captures or strictly excludes h.

A row excluding h strictly captures at least two central vertices, so it has a positive optimized-capacity Hessian direction by the central-pair Schur theorem. The joint index bound k+sum positive-index_i<=4, with k=3, allows at most one such row. Raw margins sum to zero at h, so at least one row excludes h and at least one captures it. Therefore exactly one row excludes h and two capture it.

A row capturing h must have a strict quadrilateral section. A triangular section with noncentral h isolates h; that orientation strictly captures only h, impossible at a proper full-row threshold minimum.

The row excluding h cannot have a triangular section either. Here is the needed stronger index argument. Reverse its orientation so its cap isolates h, with raw values c_h>0 and c_j<=0. Its cap fraction is

    V=c_h^3 / product_(j!=h)(c_h-c_j),
    b_j=c_h/[3(c_h-c_j)] (j!=h).

On the two-dimensional vector space v_h=0, b dot v=0, the squared-sum term in the Hessian vanishes and

    v^T Hess(V)v=V sum_(j!=h) [v_j/(c_h-c_j)]^2>0

for every nonzero v. The actual complementary cap has the negative of this Hessian. The Schur correction therefore provides a two-dimensional positive subspace for its optimized capacity. This violates the joint index bound. The formula remains valid at a through-vertex boundary because the neighboring tetrahedral cap formulas have the same derivatives through order two; their discrepancy starts at the cubic knot term. No genericity assumption is used.

Thus all three minimizing sections are strict quadrilaterals.

Orient all three raw normals toward h and normalize their h-entry to 1. The oriented normal corresponding to the actual h-excluding row lies strictly between the other two: this is the actual positive raw-margin balance divided by the h-entries. The central coordinate positive at the middle point must be positive at one endpoint. Consequently either all three have the same 2+2 split, or, after relabeling i,j,k, their actual captured pairs are exactly

    X: {h,i},        Y: {j,k},        Z: {h,j}.        (1)

Here the h-oriented versions of X and Y share the split {h,i}|{j,k}; Z has the other split. This note concerns (1), without assuming a sign for an arbitrary noncentral-pair Hessian.

## 2. All three threshold corrections can be funded simultaneously

Normalize the common positive Lagrange multiplier to have coordinate sum 1, so it equals b. Write

    t_i=b dot X_i,     c_i=t_i 1-X_i,
    P_i=Pr(sum_j c_ij Exp_j>=0),
    f_i=f_(sum_j c_ij Exp_j)(0)=P_i/t_i,
    H_i=Hess_(c_i) P_i.

The objective weight of row i in this normalization is P_i^(1/3). Let E=b^perp. For v in E define

    Q_i(v)=-v^T H_i v/(3f_i),
    kappa_i(v)=t_i^2 (1^T H_i v)/(3P_i).

The square t_i^2 is essential: H_i is in actual raw-margin coordinates. The proved optimized-threshold Schur identity says

    P_i^(1/3) (v+kappa_i(v)1)^T Hess(phi)(X_i)
                         (v+kappa_i(v)1)=Q_i(v).      (2)

Take ANY v_X,v_Y,v_Z in E with sum zero, and put K=sum_i kappa_i(v_i). The actual row motions

    delta X_i=v_i+kappa_i(v_i)1-K X_i                (3)

sum to zero. They preserve strict positivity for sufficiently small parameters. Capacity is degree one, so its Hessian annihilates the radial vector X_i. Thus all radial and radial-cross contributions in (3) vanish, and the exact weighted second variation is

    Q_X(v_X)+Q_Y(v_Y)+Q_Z(v_Z).                      (4)

Equation (4) retains each individual threshold reoptimization. It is not obtained by discarding the Schur term.

The degree-zero raw cap identity H_i c_i=-grad P_i and grad P_i=3f_i b imply that c_i is a kernel vector of the restricted bilinear form Q_i on E. Active-row rank three and c_X+c_Y+c_Z=0 imply that

    U=span(c_X,c_Z)=span(c_X,c_Y,c_Z)

is two-dimensional, and every pair of these raw vectors is independent.

## 3. The exact cost of funding the favorable row

The row Y captures two central coordinates, hence Q_Y has a positive direction. At a possible least-active maximum the joint-index theorem forces Q_X and Q_Z to be negative semidefinite on E; otherwise two full rows would already have positive index. Put

    A_X=-Q_X,       A_Z=-Q_Z,

viewed as positive semidefinite bilinear forms on the three-dimensional E. Their kernels contain c_X,c_Z respectively.

If either kernel has a vector outside U, its kernel together with the other radial kernel spans E. Every prescribed v=v_Y can then be decomposed as v=u_X+u_Z with A_X(u_X)=A_Z(u_Z)=0. Taking v_X=-u_X, v_Z=-u_Z in (4) funds the favorable row at zero cost and yields a positive second variation. Such a case is excluded immediately.

It remains to suppose both kernels are contained in U. Let ell be any nonzero linear functional on E with kernel U. Then ell belongs to the range of both A_X,A_Z. Use any Euclidean coordinates on E and define their Moore-Penrose inverses. Put

    d_X=ell^T A_X^+ ell>0,
    d_Z=ell^T A_Z^+ ell>0,
    D=d_X+d_Z.                                      (5)

For any prescribed v in E, the EXACT attained minimum is

    min_(u_X+u_Z=v) [A_X(u_X)+A_Z(u_Z)]
          =ell(v)^2/D.                              (6)

Proof: for a positive semidefinite A and ell in its range, Cauchy-Schwarz in the A inner product gives

    A(u)>=ell(u)^2/(ell^T A^+ ell).

Equality is attained by u proportional to A^+ell, with an arbitrary kernel addition. If ell(u_X)=s and ell(u_Z)=ell(v)-s, minimization of the two scalar squares gives ell(v)^2/D. Choose those two equality vectors. Their sum has the same ell-value as v, so its discrepancy from v lies in U. The radial vectors c_X,c_Z span U and lie in the corresponding kernels; adding suitable multiples corrects the discrepancy without changing either cost. This proves attainment and equality, even when either A_i has an additional kernel direction inside U.

Therefore the largest curvature available to this exact jointly corrected funding scheme is the quadratic form

    Q_eff(v)=Q_Y(v)-ell(v)^2/D.                      (7)

Every positive direction of (7) is an actual feasible improving variation of the original three rows. Conversely, for a fixed v_Y, no choice of the other two corrected directions gives more than (7). This is a precise funding criterion, not a claim that (7) is always positive somewhere.

## 4. Scalar form on the two-dimensional quotient

Both Q_Y and ell annihilate c_Y. They therefore descend to E/span(c_Y). If the descended Q_Y is nondegenerate, its positive index is exactly one at any unresolved maximum, so its signature is (+,-). Formula (7) has a positive direction if and only if

    D > ell^T Q_Y^{-1} ell.                          (8)

Indeed the matrix determinant lemma gives

    det(Q_Y-ell ell^T/D)
       =det(Q_Y)[1-(ell^T Q_Y^{-1}ell)/D].

The initial determinant is negative and subtracting a positive semidefinite rank-one matrix preserves a strictly negative direction. Thus positivity of the other direction is exactly strict negativity of this determinant, which is (8). The notation in (8) refers only to the invertible two-dimensional quotient form, not an inverse on E.

No nonsingularity is needed for the primary criterion (7). For an entirely scalar treatment of a degenerate quotient, choose a quotient basis (u,v) with ell(u)=0, ell(v)=1, and write its Q_Y matrix as [[a,c],[c,b]]. Then the funded matrix is [[a,c],[c,b-1/D]]. If a>0 it improves immediately. If a=0,c!=0 it is indefinite and improves. If a=0,c=0, its positive-index assumption gives b>0 and improvement is exactly bD>1. If a<0, completing the square gives improvement exactly

    b-c^2/a > 1/D.

These cases exhaust all quotient degeneracies and show exactly which comparison remains to be proved from actual cross-split centroid geometry.
